summary: The lease should provide specific contact details for repair emergencies.
explanation: Your lease should include contact information for reporting repairs, especially for emergencies. Without this, you might not know who to contact when urgent issues arise.
compliant_examples: For emergency repairs, contact the landlord at 01-123-4567
Maintenance issues should be reported to maintenance@property.com
For urgent repairs, call the property manager at the number provided
non_compliant_examples: No mention of how to report maintenance issues
recommended_action: Ask your landlord to provide specific contact information for reporting repairs and emergencies. Get this in writing as an addendum to your lease.

summary: The lease should mention the landlord's obligation to register the tenancy with the RTB.
explanation: All private residential tenancies must be registered with the Residential Tenancies Board (RTB). Your lease should acknowledge this legal requirement.
compliant_examples: This tenancy will be registered with the RTB as required by law
The landlord will register this tenancy with the Residential Tenancies Board
This tenancy is subject to registration under the Residential Tenancies Act
non_compliant_examples: No reference to the Residential Tenancies Board
recommended_action: Ask your landlord to confirm in writing that the tenancy will be registered with the RTB. You can verify registration by requesting the RTB registration number or checking directly with the RTB.

summary: The lease should guarantee your right to quiet and peaceful enjoyment of the property.
explanation: You have a legal right to quiet and peaceful enjoyment of your rented home without unreasonable interference from the landlord. This right should be acknowledged in your lease.
compliant_examples: The tenant has the right to peaceful and exclusive occupation of the property
The landlord guarantees the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment of the premises
The tenant shall have peaceful enjoyment of the dwelling without interference
non_compliant_examples: No reference to tenant's right to privacy
recommended_action: Request that your landlord add a clause acknowledging your right to quiet and peaceful enjoyment. Even if not explicitly stated, this right is protected by law under the Residential Tenancies Act.

summary: The lease should specify how and when rent may be reviewed or increased.
explanation: Your lease should clearly state the conditions under which rent may be increased, including the notice period required (minimum 90 days) and frequency limitations (no more than once every 12 months).
compliant_examples: Rent may be reviewed once every 12 months with 90 days' written notice
Any rent increase will be communicated with at least 90 days' notice
Rent reviews will follow RTB guidelines and provide required notice
non_compliant_examples: No mention of rent review process
No reference to notice period for rent increases
No information about frequency of rent reviews
recommended_action: Ask your landlord to include clear terms about rent reviews, including the legally required 90-day notice period and 12-month minimum between increases. Note that these protections apply even if not explicitly stated in your lease.

summary: The lease should reference an inventory and condition report of the property.
explanation: A detailed inventory and condition report documents the state of the property and its contents at the start of your tenancy. This helps prevent disputes about damage and deposit deductions when you move out.
legal_reference: Best practice under Residential Tenancies Act 2004
compliant_examples: An inventory and condition report will be completed and signed by both parties
The condition of the property is documented in the attached inventory report
A detailed inventory forms part of this agreement
non_compliant_examples: No reference to property condition documentation
recommended_action: Request a detailed inventory and condition report before moving in. Take photos of the property condition and any existing damage. Have the landlord sign and date this report to avoid future disputes about the property's original condition.
